newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU reassures applicants on membership chances.
newsitem.headline: EU reassures applicants on membership chances.

text.p: The European Commission, seeking to reassure a queue of anxious east European applicants, said on Thursday they should not take it as rejection if they were not admitted to the first round of EU membership talks.

In one of the clearest indications yet that the European Union might decide to defer talks with some of the least prepared of the 10 east European countries until later, the EU's External Relations Commissioner Hans van den Broek said staggered membership talks would not amount to discrimination.

"Too much emphasis should not be put on the question of whether the enlargement negotiations will start with all the countries at the same time or whether a differentiation will take place," he said in a speech in Switzerland.
"Differentiation in time would not mean discrimination and suggestions to that effect could become self-fulfilling in the hearts and minds of people in applicant countries."

The European Commission is currently putting the finishing touches to advice to EU governments on the state of preparedness of Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovakia, Slovenia, Bulgaria, Romania, Estonia, Lithuania and Latvia for EU entry.

It plans to finalise the documents on July 15 and hand them to EU governments, the European Parliament and the countries themselves on July 16. EU governments will decide by the end of the year with whom to open talks.
But that timetable depends on whether EU heads of government finalise at the June 16-17 EU summit in Amsterdam a new treaty overhauling the EU ready for the day it has up to 12 new members.
Van den Broek stressed on Thursday that a delay to the treaty review would be bad for the EU's enlargement plans.
"It would be bad for enlargement because widening Europe without improving its functioning is a recipe for stagnation and paralysis," he said.

Bulgarian Prime Minister Ivan Kostov -- whose country is widely regarded as being at the back of the queue in terms of preparation after years of economic and political chaos -- said he had received hopeful signs during a three-day visit to Brussels this week that talks with all countries would start at the same time.

"We were given the hope that this can be the decision which can be taken. There's no question of any guarantees at this point," the new reformist prime minister told a news conference after his first overseas visit since election.
Kostov said his new government's policy of economic and political reforms had opened a new era, but Bulgaria was still not out of the woods.
"When you've been a bad pupil you have to deserve your A (grades) several times before you get them," he said.

The EU takes its decision aware that the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation (NATO) will only invite some, and possibly only three, of 12 former eastern bloc countries to its own accession talks at its July 8-9 Madrid Summit.
Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are tipped as the three to cross the crossing line of the military alliance first.

Kostov said he had been given assurances by NATO ambassadors on Wednesday that the July summit meeting would not only be about opening talks with the lucky few, but about ways of keeping the door open to those left out.
